31:1: Now the Philistines were waging war in Israel and the men of Israel retreated from before the Philistines and fell killed on Mount Gilboa.
31:2: And the Philistines overtook Saul and his sons. And the Philistines killed Jonathan and Abinadab and Malchishua, the sons of Saul.
31:3: The wagers of war pressed hard upon Saul and the archers found him, men who were skilled at bending the bow. And he feared greatly from the archers.
31:4: Then Saul said to his armour bearer, “Draw your sword and kill me with it, lest these uncircumcised come and kill me and mock me.” But his armour bearer would not, for he feared greatly. So Saul took his own sword and fell upon it.
31:5: And when his armour bearer saw that Saul was dead, he also fell upon his sword and died with him.
31:6: Thus Saul died, and his three sons, and his armour bearer, all his men on that very day together.
31:7: And when the men of Israel, those on the other side of the valley and those on the other side of the Jordan, saw that the men of Israel had retreated and that Saul and his sons were dead, they left the cities and retreated. And the Philistines came and dwelt in them.
31:8: On the day after, when the Philistines came to strip the killed ones, they found Saul and his three sons killed, lying on Mount Gilboa.
31:9: And they cut off his head and stripped off his armour. And they sent [messengers] throughout the land of the Philistines to carry the good news into the house of their idols and to the people.
31:10: They put his armour in the house of Ashtaroth and they hung his body on the wall of Beth shan.
31:11: But when the inhabitants of Jabesh gilead heard about it – what the Philistines had done to Saul –
31:12: all the heroic men arose and went all night. They took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Beth shan. And when they came to Jabesh, they kindled for them a fire, as they used to kindle for the kings there.
31:13: And they took their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh, and fasted seven days.

n: T
After God’s Spirit left Saul, his rule continued to fail. His time as king ended in shame and military defeat ({{1 Samuel 31:1-13|1 Samuel 31}}).
B

David and his men weren’t safe in Israel. A Philistine king gave them a town to live in. It was very hard for David not to live among the Israelites. Not being allowed to live in Israel was one of the covenant curses. Yet David was always faithful to God and worshipped only God.

Then the Amalekites destroyed David’s town. They captured David’s families’ and the families of his men. David and his soldiers were very sad and bitter about this. God helped them to get their families and belongings back. That happened while the Philistines went to attack the Israelites.

Saul was very afraid of the Philistine army. He tried to receive advice from God through dreams, prophets and casting lots. But he had refused to believe the words God had already told him through Samuel. Then he asked for help from a woman who was a medium. This means that she talked to spirits. She talked to the spiritual part of people whose bodies had died.

Samuel’s spirit told Saul the same things Samuel had told Saul before. Saul’s family line would no longer rule as kings. Saul, Jonathan and two of Saul’s other sons died in the battle against the Philistines. David was far away and wasn’t guilty of Saul’s death. After Saul died, the people of Jabesh Gilead honoured his body. They were the people Saul had rescued in his first battle as king.
T

- The Israelites fled southeast from the Valley of Jezreel ({{1 Samuel 29:1|1 Samuel 29:1}}) to higher and hillier areas. With their chariots, the Philistines had the advantage in the more level valley. 

- Mount Gilboa is southwest of the Sea of Galilee, far from the territory of the Philistines.
T
While David was in the south successfully fighting the Amalekites ({{1 Samuel 30:1-31|1 Samuel 30}}), Saul was in the north unsuccessfully fighting the Philistines.
T
*Jonathan … Malkishua*: See {{1 Samuel 14:49|1 Samuel 14:49}}. This is the first mention of Saul’s son Abinadab (compare {{1 Chronicles 8:33|1 Chronicles 8:33}}; {{1 Chronicles 9:39|9:39}}).
T

- David had earlier served as an armor bearer (a personal assistant who carried a soldier’s weapons) to Saul ({{1 Samuel 16:21|1 Samuel 16:21}}). 

- *run me through*: This is one of many similarities between the death of Abimelech during the time of the judges ({{Judges 9:1-57|Judges 9}}) and Saul, Israel’s first national king (see {{Judges 9:54|Judges 9:54}}). In both stories, a wounded leader asks someone else to kill him rather than die in shame.
T
After a victory, the army would remove items from the dead. They searched the bodies for anything valuable, such as clothing, weapons, or jewelry.
T

In the ancient world, people saw the death of an enemy king as good news. They believed it meant that the enemy’s god had been defeated. The Philistines did not realize that their victory would not last and would bring them no real gain. David, the Lord’s true anointed king, would soon come to power and defeat the Philistines. Instead of defeating Israel’s God, the Philistines were unknowingly carrying out his purpose.
T

- *the Ashtoreths*: See {{1 Samuel 7:3|1 Samuel 7:3}}.

- *hung his body*: This act further humiliated the executed person by denying them a proper burial. It also served as a warning to other potential enemies (see also {{Genesis 40:19|Genesis 40:19}}; {{Deuteronomy 21:21-22|Deuteronomy 21:21–22}}; {{Joshua 10:26|Joshua 10:26}}; {{Esther 9:6-14|Esther 9:6–14}}). 

- Beth-shan was a short distance east of Mount Gilboa.
T

The people of Jabesh-gilead were repaying a kindness. Earlier, Saul had rescued them from the Ammonites and their king Nahash ({{1 Samuel 11:1-13|1 Samuel 11:1–13}}). Jabesh-gilead was about nineteen kilometers (twelve miles) southeast of Beth-shan. It lay across the Jordan River.
T
*burned the bodies*: Cremation was uncommon in the ancient world. The bodies may have been burned because decomposition had already begun.
T

- *bones … Jabesh*: This was not where Saul's remains were finally laid to rest (see {{2 Samuel 21:12-14|2 Samuel 21:12–14}}).

- The end of 1 Samuel returns Israel's history to the time at the end of Judges, when “Israel had no king.” The Philistines were in control again. David had God’s anointing but no crown. He had wives but no sons. His connection with the hated Philistines may have put his standing with his own people at risk. David's future would be difficult. Still, it was clear that God was with him.
